stories.headline: NVIDIA SURGES ~30% AS BOARD REINSTATES HUANG, FUELING BEST MARKET DAY SINCE APRIL 2025
stories.body: Nvidia shares jumped roughly 30%, adding close to $1 trillion in market value, after the board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, president and director just 11 days after his abrupt resignation; the S&P 500 rallied 4.61% to 7,237 and the Nasdaq 100 gained 6.71% to 26,746, the biggest single-day gains for both indexes since April 2025 and a sharp reversal from Friday's close in correction territory.
stories.explain: Nvidia's multi-trillion-dollar market cap and outsized weighting in both benchmarks mean its single-stock swings mechanically move cap-weighted indices far more than an equal-weighted market would — a roughly 30% rally in the largest constituent of the Nasdaq 100 alone explains most of today's 6.71% index gain. The move also resolves, for now, the leadership vacuum that had compounded the AI-capex selloff of the past two weeks, stripping out company-specific uncertainty even though the stock remains about 30% below its October 6 record.

stories.headline: TRUMP PRESSURE PRECEDED REVERSAL; HUANG'S DEC. 1 HOUSE TESTIMONY STAYS ON THE CALENDAR
stories.body: President Trump had publicly pushed Nvidia's board to bring Huang back, and today's reversal comes just over a week after directors said unanimously they had no plans to reinstate him; Huang's closed-door, transcribed interview before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China select committees over his ties to a businesswoman U.S. intelligence suspects of links to Chinese espionage remains scheduled for Dec. 1, with general counsel Tim Teter following Dec. 2.
stories.explain: A sitting CEO testifying before national-security-focused committees is a materially different proposition than a departed executive doing the same: Congress can now press him on current company decisions, not just the circumstances of a resignation, which raises the stakes of that hearing for the stock. The board's reversal under visible political pressure also reopens a governance question for investors — whether Nvidia's directors can hold a personnel line against outside pressure is itself a risk factor the market has to start pricing alongside the AI-capex story.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD BARELY MOVES TO 4.92% DESPITE THE RISK-ON SURGE, POINTING TO AN EQUITY-SPECIFIC UNWIND
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield was essentially flat at 4.92% (+1 bp) even as stocks posted their best day in over a year, a muted bond-market reaction that suggests today's rally is concentrated in resolving single-stock and sector-specific uncertainty rather than a broad repricing of growth or Fed policy.
stories.explain: If today's move reflected a genuine upgrade to the macro growth outlook, yields would typically rise as investors rotated out of safe Treasuries and priced in a less dovish Fed path; instead the near-flat yield shows bond investors treating this as idiosyncratic corporate news rather than new information about GDP, inflation, or the Dec. 8-9 FOMC decision. That divergence matters for the week ahead: Wednesday's October core PCE print, not Monday's equity relief rally, remains the actual swing factor for yields and hike odds.

stories.headline: DECEMBER HIKE ODDS STAY ELEVATED HEADING INTO WEDNESDAY'S CORE PCE, RELEASED EARLY FOR THANKSGIVING
stories.body: Fed funds futures continue to price a meaningfully above-even chance of a quarter-point hike at the Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting, with the funds rate still at 3.75%-4.00%; the October core PCE report lands Wednesday, Nov. 25 — pulled forward a day ahead of Thursday's Thanksgiving holiday — making it the last major inflation read before the decision, followed by the November jobs report on Dec. 4.
stories.explain: Core PCE is the Fed's explicitly preferred inflation gauge because it strips out volatile food and energy prices and adjusts for consumers substituting toward cheaper goods, giving policymakers a cleaner read on underlying price pressure than CPI. Because it is the last PCE print before the meeting and arrives compressed against the holiday calendar, a hot number has outsized power to cement hike odds already running high, while a soft one would be the clearest remaining chance to unwind them before the FOMC meets.

stories.headline: GOLD AND DOLLAR TICK HIGHER, OIL SLIDES 3.86% AS HAVEN FLOWS DECOUPLE FROM THE EQUITY REBOUND
stories.body: Gold added 0.73% to about $3,634 an ounce and the dollar index rose 0.56% to 104.35 even as WTI crude slipped 3.86% to roughly $80 a barrel, a mixed commodities tape showing haven positioning from last week's selloff unwinding only partially even as equities staged their sharpest rally in over a year.
stories.explain: Gold rising alongside a firmer dollar is the less common pairing — the two typically move inversely since gold is dollar-denominated — which suggests today's gold bid is residual safe-haven demand left over from last week's AI-capex scare rather than a currency effect. Oil's decline even as stocks surged is the clearer signal that crude traders are pricing supply and demand fundamentals independently of the Nvidia-driven equity story, which is why commodities didn't simply mirror Monday's stock-market surge.

watchlist: Oct. core PCE inflation — Wed., Nov. 25, 8:30 AM ET, released a day early ahead of Thanksgiving and the last major print before the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting
Jensen Huang's closed-door House testimony — Dec. 1, now as a sitting CEO rather than a departed one, with GC Tim Teter following Dec. 2
November jobs report — Dec. 4, four days before the FOMC decision
Fed's Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting — hike odds elevated with the funds rate at 3.75%-4.00%
Nvidia follow-through — watch whether Monday's ~30% rally holds or fades as a one-day relief bounce; shares remain roughly 30% below their Oct. 6 record

deepDive.title: Key-Person Risk and Index Math: What Nvidia's Reinstatement Rally Reveals About Cap-Weighted Benchmarks
content: Monday's market move is unusual in its cause: the S&P 500's best day since April 2025 and the Nasdaq 100's best day in even longer were driven overwhelmingly by a single corporate personnel decision — Nvidia's board reversing course and reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO. That is worth slowing down on, because it is a clean, almost laboratory-grade example of a phenomenon finance students read about in the abstract but rarely see this starkly: key-person risk compounded by index concentration. Understanding the mechanics of how one stock moved two major benchmarks by four to seven percent in a single session explains a lot about how passive index investing actually works today.

The mechanism is pure arithmetic. A cap-weighted index's daily return is the sum of each constituent's weight multiplied by its own return. Nvidia's weight in the Nasdaq 100 has run near 13-15% in 2026, and in the S&P 500 near 7-8%, reflecting a market capitalization that has at times exceeded $4 trillion. A roughly 30% single-day gain in a stock with a 14% index weight contributes over four points of index return almost by itself — which is most of the Nasdaq 100's 6.71% gain today, before any other constituent moves. This is why a handful of 'Magnificent Seven'-type names can now swing a diversified-sounding index the way a single sector used to require dozens of stocks to do.

What gets missed is that this concentration cuts both ways and compounds with correlation. Nvidia's weight didn't appear overnight; it built up over several years as investors crowded into the same AI-infrastructure thesis, which means Nvidia-correlated names (AMD, the hyperscalers, memory makers) tend to move with it, amplifying the effect further. The closest historical parallel is Apple in the early 2010s, when health-related uncertainty about Steve Jobs repeatedly moved the stock by mid-single digits and visibly dented the Nasdaq on days with no other news — except Apple's index weight then was smaller than Nvidia's is now, and AI-era valuations have made earnings and leadership narratives even more reflexive with price.

For today's setup, the lesson cuts two ways. First, index-level statistics like 'the S&P rallied 4.61%' can conceal that breadth was narrow — a student should always check whether a market move was broad-based or a single-name event before drawing conclusions about the economy. Second, the governance reversal itself introduces a new, harder-to-model risk: a board that changes a CEO decision under public and political pressure within two weeks signals that Nvidia's leadership stability — and by extension a meaningful slice of major-index returns — is now partly a function of political dynamics, not just AI-capex fundamentals, right as Huang heads into a sitting-CEO congressional appearance on Dec. 1.
